introduction: Are not all Christians Bahá’ís? The guide opens with that question and with an answer that turns on conduct: whoever acts wholly by the teachings of Christ is what the name means. The readings then speak of Christ as the Word, explain the bread from heaven, baptism and the rock, follow fishermen who did what philosophers could not, and trace a religion that joined hostile peoples, outlasted emperors, and was afterwards altered by leaders allied with princes. They end by setting the Sermon on the Mount beside nations at war. Because the readings comment on the Gospels, the Gospel passages are given here as they stand, and the reader can judge the commentary: the Word made flesh, “this is my body”, “upon this rock”, “put up again thy sword”. The Qur’an speaks beside them of a Messiah who is a messenger and a word from God. Then come those who see it otherwise. Thomas says “my Lord and my God” and the Council of Nicaea “of one substance with the Father”; Paul forbids any other gospel; Tertullian asks what Athens has to do with Jerusalem; Augustine allows war as a necessity; Madison trusts a multiplicity of sects; Gibbon, Swift and Dostoevsky look at what the Church became. It is a conversation Christians have long had among themselves, joined here from outside.
questions: “When Christians act according to the teachings of Christ, they are called Bahá’ís.” What does this answer assume about names and communities, and how would a Christian who holds Paul’s “no other gospel” respond?

The readings explain “the Word” by words and letters. Set this beside John’s prologue, the creed of Nicaea, Thomas’s confession and the Qur’an’s “no other than a messenger”. Where exactly do these accounts differ?
The bread from heaven, baptism and the Eucharist are read here as figures. What in the Gospel passages supports such readings, and what resists them?
After Christ there were dissensions, the readings say, because no centre was appointed. What do Paul’s “I am of Paul”, Milton and Madison each make of religious division?
The readings credit Christ with uniting the peoples and learning of the ancient world. How do Tertullian’s question, Gibbon’s sentence and Swift’s complaint qualify that picture?
“Christ forbade war!” Read the sheathed sword and the other cheek with Augustine’s letter to a general, Twain’s War Prayer and Owen’s anthem. Has the teaching been forgotten, or interpreted?

outside.why: “When Christians act according to the teachings of Christ, they are called Bahá’ís.” The Gospel had already made conduct, and one kind of conduct, the mark of a disciple: by this shall all know you, if you love one another.
The reading makes acting on the teachings the test of who is what. Jesus says the same of those who call him Lord and do not do the Father’s will.

“Are not all Christians Bahá’ís?” The answer treats the two names as one thing rightly lived. Juliet thought a name no part of the thing named. If the rose is the same, why have the names divided people so deeply?
Beside a dead animal the disciples see only what is foul, and Christ remarks on its white teeth. The Gospel’s saying about the mote and the beam teaches the same discipline of the eye.
“Christ’s sovereignty was spiritual sovereignty … His dominions were hearts.” He says so to the Roman governor: my kingdom is not of this world, or my servants would fight.

The reading sets Christ’s reign in hearts above the conquests of Napoleon and Genghis Khan. Machiavelli, studying how new orders are founded, concluded that unarmed prophets are destroyed. Which of them has the history of Christianity borne out?

Christ, says the reading, knew that his Cause “would antagonize all the peoples of the earth” and accepted what followed. Christians have read the servant of Isaiah as that acceptance: despised, rejected, wounded for others.
The question is how the human spirit proceeds from God, “since in the Torah it is said that God breathed the spirit into the body of man”. This is the verse.
The reading calls Christ “the all-encompassing Word of God”. The title is from the opening of John’s Gospel.

The Word and the Most Great Name, the reading says, “have appeared with a revelation beyond all compare”. The believers of the Qur’an say that they make no distinction between any of God’s messengers. Can one both rank the messengers and refuse to?
“Jesus, son of Mary, was naught but a Messenger before whom other Messengers had passed away.” The Báb’s sentence is the Qur’an’s, nearly word for word.
The reading names Muḥammad “the Seal of the Prophets”. This is the verse from which the title comes.

“He was but a Messenger of God and the first of them that worship.” Thomas, in John’s Gospel, addresses the risen Jesus as “my Lord and my God”, and is not corrected. What is each tradition protecting in the way it speaks of him?
“As Christ conveyed the perfect meaning of divine reality … He was the Word.” John’s sentence is the source: the Word was made flesh, and dwelt among us.

The reading explains “the Word” by the difference between a word, which has meaning, and letters, which have none alone. The bishops at Nicaea explained it in terms of substance: begotten, not made, of one substance with the Father. What does each explanation make of the distance between Christ and other people?
“The Letter is a member of the Word” and draws its value from it. Paul’s figure for the same dependence is a body, in which the eye cannot say to the hand, I have no need of thee.
The Apostles are letters whose worth comes from the Word. In John they are branches of a vine, and a branch apart from it bears nothing.
“The reality of Christ, Who is the Word of God, undoubtedly precedes all created things.” The Letter to the Colossians: he is before all things, and by him all things consist.
While in the world he was “despised and reviled”, crowned with thorns. Isaiah’s servant has no form or comeliness and no beauty that anyone should desire him.

“The honour and greatness of Christ reside not in His being without a father.” Luke’s account of the annunciation is the passage in question; the reading asks that it not be made the ground of his greatness.
“Jesus Christ had brothers. (It is understood that they did not believe in Him).” John says so in passing.
The reading discusses the household of Jesus. His townspeople used that household against him: the carpenter, whose brothers and sisters we know.
The reading quotes it: “Why callest thou me good?” Here is the exchange in Mark.
“The body is the word. The spirit is its meaning. The word passes. The spirit remains.” Paul’s contrast of letter and spirit is near kin to this.
“The word passes”, says the reading. Jesus says that heaven and earth shall pass away, but his words shall not. In what sense does a scripture’s wording pass, and in what sense does it stay?
“The Lord of Hosts became manifest … in a pillar of fire.” Exodus describes it leading Israel by night.
The reading explains “I am the living bread which came down from heaven”. In John the saying at once divides its hearers, who ask how this man can give his flesh to eat.
To eat the bread from heaven, the reading says, is to guide and be guided. Jesus gives the key in the same chapter: the flesh profits nothing; the words are spirit and life.

“Some imagine that the bread of the Eucharist is the reality of Christ”, an error in the reading’s eyes. The words on which that belief rests are these, spoken at the last supper. How should a sentence as plain as “this is my body” be read?
Christ submitted to John’s baptism, the reading says, “that the law which had issued from the former religion might be fulfilled”. His own explanation to John is the same.
“Outwardly he was but an humble artisan, his disciples simple fishermen.” The council in Jerusalem made the same observation, and could explain the disciples’ boldness only by where they had been.
Why could fishermen do what philosophers could not? Paul asks the Corinthians to look at themselves: not many wise, mighty or noble, and chosen for that reason.
The Apostles “spoke with all peoples as if in their own tongue”. Acts tells it as the event of Pentecost; the reading takes the tongues as a way of speaking to every kind of person.
Christ asks who he is, and Peter answers. This is the question and the answer.
“Thou art the rock and upon this rock I build my church”: one word, the reading says, that dispelled differences. This is the passage, with the keys that follow.
“There were dissensions after the departure of Christ because there had been no Center appointed.” Paul is already writing against them within a generation: I am of Paul, I of Apollos, I of Cephas.

The reading counts the sects that arose after Christ as “childish attempts”. Milton saw in a multitude of opinions the sign of a people learning, since opinion in good men is knowledge in the making. Is division always a failure?

One point has now been designated, the reading says, “so that no differences would remain”. Madison held that religious liberty is safest where sects are many and none can command. What protects conscience in a community with a single centre?
The aim is that no differences remain. Jesus prays for it on the last night: that they all may be one.
“The tests made Peter the Apostle deny Christ.” A few hours before, he had promised that he never would.
“Christ had raised up twelve men and four women.” Luke names some of the women who travelled with him and paid his way.

The reading compares the short ministry of Christ with the long one of Moses and its “physical rules”. John draws the line between them in a sentence: the law by Moses, grace and truth by Jesus Christ.
In this cycle, the reading says, “universal peace will prevail; bloodshed and war will cease”. The promise is Micah’s: swords into ploughshares, and no one afraid.

The reading names universal peace as what distinguishes this Revelation from that of Christ. Jesus said of his own coming that it would bring not peace but a sword. Does that saying describe a purpose or a consequence?
“The teachings of Jesus are in a concentrated form.” He said as much: there were many things his disciples could not yet bear.
The message of Bahá’u’lláh, says the reading, “is the medicine of which the world has much need”, as Christ’s was in its season. The physician is his own figure for himself.

“We act in accordance with the Gospel. But we must also act in accordance with the teachings of Bahá’u’lláh.” Paul forbade the Galatians any other gospel, even from an angel. How would the reading answer a Christian who quotes him?
Christ “unified the various peoples and nations of the world”. Paul states the result in the churches he knew: neither Jew nor Greek, bond nor free, male nor female.
“He taught mankind by the power of the Holy Spirit and not through human agency.” The first hearers of the Sermon on the Mount felt the difference from their scribes.
“They were dark, they became illumined.” Matthew applies Isaiah’s words to the beginning of the ministry in Galilee: the people that walked in darkness have seen a great light.
Christ “welded together a people” from Roman, Greek, Egyptian and Syrian. The Letter to the Ephesians says it of Jew and Gentile: he has broken down the middle wall of partition.
Christ, the reading says, “cemented together the sciences of Rome and the splendors of the civilization of Greece”. Paul at Athens begins the work, starting from an altar of theirs.

The reading credits Christ with joining the learning of Greece and Rome to faith. Tertullian, a Christian writing about the year 200, wanted no such join: what has Athens to do with Jerusalem? Which of them describes what Christianity became?
God raised Christ among a subject people and “breathed the spirit of life into them, and revived them after their death”. Ezekiel’s valley of bones is the picture behind such language.

Through Jesus “all sects and creeds and nations were taught the beauty of unity”. Swift, a dean of the Church seventeen centuries later, thought the lesson half learned at best: enough religion to hate, not enough to love. What happened between the teaching and the taught?

Christ, “solitary and alone”, the reading says, “achieved divine conquests in the fields of the West”. Gibbon describes the same conquest in one long sentence and then asks by what human causes it came about. Do his causes and the reading’s exclude each other?
Nations and peoples became “submissive and lowly before a Word”. Daniel saw one like a son of man given a dominion that all peoples and languages would serve.
The Faith of Jesus appeared in the East, and only in the West showed “the full measure of its potentialities”. His own image for it is the smallest seed, which becomes a tree.
“Without schooling or outward education and trained to labor in the shop of a carpenter.” Jerusalem asked how this man knew letters, having never learned.

One man is so exalted that others “bow down before Him and He is adored by them like Christ or Moses”; another bows to dust. The commandment given through Moses forbids bowing to anything but God. How does the reading distinguish the two bowings?
“Christ always used to cross this Mount Carmel, Haifa and Nazareth.” The Gospels remember him as always on the road, with nowhere to lay his head.
The reading cites the “melodies” in Matthew that herald the advent after him. This is the passage: the sun darkened, the stars falling, the Son of man in the clouds.

For the reading these signs are figures of a later Manifestation. The disciples at the Ascension were told that Jesus himself would come again “in like manner”. What decides between a return of the person and the coming of another?
Christ was rejected because the expected signs had not appeared, among them where the Messiah should come from. John records the objection as it was made: shall Christ come out of Galilee?
“The teachings of Moses were like a seed … the fruit signified Christ.” Jesus makes the claim to those who trusted in Moses: he wrote of me.
Christ is “the result of all the teachings of Moses”. He says that he came not to destroy the law but to fulfil it.

“There are two kinds of Love: one Universal and one Individual”; the first is commanded, the second “cannot be forced”. A character in Dostoevsky finds the first easy and the second nearly impossible. Which of the two does the love commanded in the Gospels most resemble?
“Even if they kill you, you must love them.” The Sermon on the Mount gives the command and its reason: the Father sends rain on the just and on the unjust.
The Romans and Greeks thought they had no need of the Cause, having “a perfect civilization”. Paul knew that judgment: to the Greeks, who seek wisdom, the preaching was foolishness.
“Jesus Christ gave His life upon the cross for the unity of mankind.” He names the measure of such a gift himself.
“Though the Jews put Him to death, that martyrdom” proved potent in the world. Tertullian said of the martyrs who followed that their blood is seed.

“The kings and emperors of the world could not resist its spread.” The second psalm, which the first Christians applied to their own case, has the kings of the earth set against the Lord’s anointed and the Lord laughing.
The reading recalls the persecutions under the emperors. The Beatitude had told the persecuted what to make of them.
A king “realized that no matter how many Christians were slain, it bore no fruit”, and stopped. Gamaliel had given that advice at the very beginning: let them alone.

The sepulchre of Christ, the reading says, was a rubbish dump for three hundred years until a church was built on it. The women who came to the tomb on the first morning were asked why they sought the living among the dead. What is honoured when a tomb is honoured?

The reading takes the crucifixion as a fact on which Jews and Christians agree, and differs from them about its meaning. The Qur’an has a verse that most Muslims have read as denying the fact: they slew him not, but it appeared so to them. What does each account need the event to have been?
Christians, says the reading, believe in a crucified Christ who ascended. Paul says how much hangs on it: if Christ be not risen, faith is vain.
The reading quotes it: none ascends to heaven but he who came down from heaven. This is the verse, spoken while he stood on earth.
“Christ is ever in the world of existence. He has never disappeared out of it.” The last words of Matthew’s Gospel are that promise: I am with you always.
“Rest assured that Christ is present.” The Gospel names the least gathering at which that is true.
Bahá’u’lláh “called Him the Word of God, the Spirit of God”. The titles are those the Qur’an gives him; here the angels announce to Mary “a word from Him”.
‘Abdu’l-Bahá proves the validity of Christ, and “these Christians dislike me very much”. Jesus had a proverb for it.
The reading compares the spiritual life of two ages. The Qur’an allows that some messengers were raised above others in degree.

“I believe he was a great philosopher.” “Oh, no! He was much greater than a philosopher. He was the Word of God.” Emerson gave a third answer: that Jesus was the one man true to what is in every person. What does each answer ask of the one who gives it?

The reading describes the Church of the Resurrection divided among the sects. At the cross the soldiers would not tear the seamless coat, and cast lots for it whole. What have Christians done with what the soldiers left in one piece?
Under “ignorant priests”, the laws of the Evangel gave way. The charge had been made once before, in the Gospel, against another priesthood: the commandment of God set aside for the tradition of men.
“The leaders allied with princes. The foundation of Christ was completely altered.” Acton, a Catholic historian writing of popes, put the mechanism in a sentence.

Traditions prevailed, says the reading, and the divine teachings were lost. Dostoevsky imagined the returned Christ arrested by the Church’s own inquisitor and told that he had no right to add anything.
“The Christians are today submerged in the sea of imitation.” The Gospel’s word for leaders and led in that condition is blind.
“Christ forbade war! … ‘Put up thy sword into the sheath’.” This is the scene in Matthew.
The reading quotes Matthew 5:39. Here it is with the old rule it replaces.

“The teachings of Christ are forgotten”, the reading says, when Christians fight. Augustine, writing to a Christian general, did not think so: war may be waged as a necessity, in order that peace may be obtained. Was the tradition of the just war a forgetting of the Sermon on the Mount, or a reading of it?
Christ taught that one “must return good for evil”. Paul hands the teaching on: be not overcome of evil, but overcome evil with good.
Christians are “leading their young men into war … causing mothers to lose their sons”. Mark Twain wrote out what a congregation’s prayer for victory asks for when it is said in full.
“What has all this to do with the teachings of Christ?” Wilfred Owen, an officer killed in the First World War, asked what bells and prayers there were for those who die as cattle.

The average Westerner, the reading says, “is not a Christian; he is a secular churchman”, repeating what he will not live. The letter to the church at Sardis says: thou hast a name that thou livest, and art dead.
“These swords strike at Christ. These bullets are aimed at Christ.” In Matthew’s judgment scene whatever is done to the least is done to him.

The Lamb of God, says the reading, defended himself with his horns, that is, his utterances. Isaiah’s lamb is silent before the shearers and opens not his mouth. When did Jesus answer, and when did he keep silence?
The owner of an orchard “will not leave a withered tree in the garden”. This is the parable; in Luke the gardener asks for one more year.
“When Jesus Christ came to this world, He planted a tree. I have come to see what has become of that tree.” He had said how any tree is to be judged.

leftOut.saying: “I like your Christ, I do not like your Christians. Your Christians are so unlike your Christ.”
leftOut.reason: Wanted beside the readings that set the teachings of Christ against the conduct of Christians, and left out: no speech, letter or article of Gandhi’s has it. Swift’s “just enough religion to make us hate” stands in the guide instead.

genesis-breath-of-life.text: And the Lord God formed man of the dust of the ground, and breathed into his nostrils the breath of life; and man became a living soul

luke-power-of-the-highest.text: Then said Mary unto the angel, How shall this be, seeing I know not a man? And the angel answered and said unto her, The Holy Ghost shall come upon thee, and the power of the Highest shall overshadow thee: therefore also that holy thing which shall be born of thee shall be called the Son of God

exodus-pillar-of-fire.text: And the Lord went before them by day in a pillar of a cloud, to lead them the way; and by night in a pillar of fire, to give them light; to go by day and night

john-living-bread.text: I am the living bread which came down from heaven: if any man eat of this bread, he shall live for ever: and the bread that I will give is my flesh, which I will give for the life of the world. The Jews therefore strove among themselves, saying, How can this man give us his flesh to eat

matthew-this-is-my-body.text: And as they were eating, Jesus took bread, and blessed it, and brake it, and gave it to the disciples, and said, Take, eat; this is my body. And he took the cup, and gave thanks, and gave it to them, saying, Drink ye all of it; For this is my blood of the new testament, which is shed for many for the remission of sins

matthew-fulfil-all-righteousness.text: Then cometh Jesus from Galilee to Jordan unto John, to be baptized of him. But John forbad him, saying, I have need to be baptized of thee, and comest thou to me? And Jesus answering said unto him, Suffer it to be so now: for thus it becometh us to fulfil all righteousness. Then he suffered him

matthew-upon-this-rock.text: And I say also unto thee, That thou art Peter, and upon this rock I will build my church; and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it. And I will give unto thee the keys of the kingdom of heaven: and whatsoever thou shalt bind on earth shall be bound in heaven: and whatsoever thou shalt loose on earth shall be loosed in heaven

luke-certain-women.text: And it came to pass afterward, that he went throughout every city and village, preaching and shewing the glad tidings of the kingdom of God: and the twelve were with him, And certain women, which had been healed of evil spirits and infirmities, Mary called Magdalene, out of whom went seven devils, And Joanna the wife of Chuza Herod's steward, and Susanna, and many others, which ministered unto him of their substance

john-grace-and-truth.text: For the law was given by Moses, but grace and truth came by Jesus Christ

ephesians-middle-wall.text: For he is our peace, who hath made both one, and hath broken down the middle wall of partition between us

john-out-of-galilee.text: Others said, This is the Christ. But some said, Shall Christ come out of Galilee? Hath not the scripture said, That Christ cometh of the seed of David, and out of the town of Bethlehem, where David was

john-greater-love.text: Greater love hath no man than this, that a man lay down his life for his friends

psalm-heathen-rage.text: Why do the heathen rage, and the people imagine a vain thing? The kings of the earth set themselves, and the rulers take counsel together, against the Lord, and against his anointed, saying, Let us break their bands asunder, and cast away their cords from us. He that sitteth in the heavens shall laugh: the Lord shall have them in derision

luke-living-among-the-dead.text: Why seek ye the living among the dead? He is not here, but is risen

john-came-down-from-heaven.text: And no man hath ascended up to heaven, but he that came down from heaven, even the Son of man which is in heaven

luke-no-prophet-accepted.text: Verily I say unto you, No prophet is accepted in his own country

john-coat-without-seam.text: Then the soldiers, when they had crucified Jesus, took his garments, and made four parts, to every soldier a part; and also his coat: now the coat was without seam, woven from the top throughout. They said therefore among themselves, Let us not rend it, but cast lots for it, whose it shall be

matthew-put-up-thy-sword.text: And, behold, one of them which were with Jesus stretched out his hand, and drew his sword, and struck a servant of the high priest's, and smote off his ear. Then said Jesus unto him, Put up again thy sword into his place: for all they that take the sword shall perish with the sword

revelation-name-that-thou-livest.text: I know thy works, that thou hast a name that thou livest, and art dead

isaiah-lamb-to-the-slaughter.text: He was oppressed, and he was afflicted, yet he opened not his mouth: he is brought as a lamb to the slaughter, and as a sheep before her shearers is dumb, so he openeth not his mouth

quran-messiah-no-other-than-a-messenger.text: The Messiah, son of Mary, was no other than a messenger, messengers (the like of whom) had passed away before him. And his mother was a saintly woman. And they both used to eat (earthly) food

quran-crucified-him-not.text: they slew him not nor crucified him, but it appeared so unto them

quran-word-from-him.text: (And remember) when the angels said: O Mary! Lo! Allah giveth thee glad tidings of a word from him, whose name is the Messiah, Jesus, son of Mary, illustrious in the world and the Hereafter, and one of those brought near (unto Allah).

tertullian-athens-and-jerusalem.text: What indeed has Athens to do with Jerusalem? What concord is there between the Academy and the Church?
tertullian-athens-and-jerusalem.author: Tertullian

augustine-war-as-necessity.text: Peace should be the object of your desire; war should be waged only as a necessity, and waged only that God may by it deliver men from the necessity and preserve them in peace. For peace is not sought in order to the kindling of war, but war is waged in order that peace may be obtained
augustine-war-as-necessity.author: Augustine of Hippo

gibbon-banner-of-the-cross.text: a pure and humble religion gently insinuated itself into the minds of men, grew up in silence and obscurity, derived new vigour from opposition, and finally erected the triumphant banner of the cross on the ruins of the Capitol
gibbon-banner-of-the-cross.author: Edward Gibbon
gibbon-banner-of-the-cross.work: The History of the Decline and Fall of the Roman Empire
